_comment: Shared urology steps (endoscopic bladder access, resection platform, chip evacuation, perforation check, three-way catheter). Used by TURP, TURBT and suprapubic catheter insertion. Procedure-only steps live in each procedure's steps_local.

step.uro.cystoscopy.title: Urethrocystoscopy and systematic bladder inspection
step.uro.cystoscopy.why: Every endoscopic bladder operation starts with a complete map. A tumour, stone, diverticulum or ureteric orifice that is not seen at the start is the one that gets resected, missed or perforated later.
how: Pass the cystoscope under direct vision along the whole urethra, inspecting it as you go; never advance blind against resistance.
Note the length and occlusion of the prostatic urethra, the verumontanum, and the bladder neck.
Inspect the entire bladder systematically with the 30 and 70 degree lenses: dome, walls, trigone, both ureteric orifices and the bladder neck, with the bladder moderately filled.
Record the findings as a diagram before any resection begins.
pitfalls: Missing the dome and the anterior wall because the bladder was overfilled or the lens never rotated upwards.
Forcing the instrument through a stricture or a high bladder neck and creating a false passage.

step.uro.resectoscope.title: Resectoscope set-up, irrigation fluid and urethral calibration
step.uro.resectoscope.why: The choice of energy and irrigation fluid decides whether a patient can develop TUR syndrome, and an under-calibrated urethra is where post-operative strictures come from.
how: Confirm the energy platform with the team. Monopolar resection needs a non-conducting, non-haemolytic fluid such as glycine; bipolar resection uses normal saline.
Hang the irrigant at a height that gives a clear view at the lowest pressure needed; higher pressure increases fluid absorption.
Lubricate generously and calibrate the urethra gently with sounds or an Otis urethrotome if the sheath does not pass easily; do not force the sheath.
Introduce the sheath with the obturator, then the working element under vision, and check the loop, the return of fluid and the diathermy settings before the first cut.
pitfalls: Using saline with a monopolar loop. It does not cut, and the team turns the power up instead of checking the fluid.
A sheath forced through a tight meatus, leaving a meatal or bulbar stricture.

step.uro.chip-evacuation.title: Chip evacuation and specimen collection
step.uro.chip-evacuation.why: Retained chips block the catheter and cause clot retention in recovery, and every chip is tissue the pathologist needs for staging or for an incidental cancer.
how: Evacuate the chips with an Ellik evacuator or a bladder syringe through the sheath until no further fragments return.
Re-inspect the bladder for remaining chips, especially in the dome and behind the bladder neck.
Collect all fragments for histology; label separately any specimen that needs its own report.
structuresAtRisk: Bladder wall (vigorous evacuation through a perforation)
pitfalls: Aggressive Ellik pressure when a perforation is suspected, pushing fluid and chips outside the bladder.
Declaring the bladder empty without looking.

step.uro.perforation-check.title: Final inspection: perforation, orifices and landmarks
step.uro.perforation-check.why: A perforation recognised in theatre changes the plan and is usually manageable; one recognised in recovery presents as abdominal distension, pain and fluid overload, and costs time the patient may not have.
how: Inspect the resected area at low pressure: fat seen through the capsule or bladder wall, or black space beyond, means perforation.
Check that both ureteric orifices are intact and that the verumontanum and external sphincter are preserved.
Feel the abdomen under the drapes: new distension or firmness suggests extravasation.
State the findings to the anaesthetist: extent of resection, any perforation, and the time on irrigation.
pitfalls: Finishing the case because it is nearly finished when a perforation is seen.
Not telling the anaesthetist, who is the person most likely to see the first sign of absorption.

step.uro.three-way-catheter.title: Three-way catheter and continuous irrigation
step.uro.three-way-catheter.why: After a resection the bladder must stay empty and free of clot while the raw surface stops oozing. A blocked catheter in recovery means clot retention, pain and secondary bleeding.
how: Pass a three-way irrigating catheter of adequate size over an introducer if needed, confirming free drainage before inflating the balloon.
Inflate the balloon with sterile water to the volume the manufacturer specifies, and record catheter type, size and balloon volume in the note.
Start continuous irrigation with normal saline and confirm a light pink return before leaving theatre.
Hand over the irrigation plan and the input-output chart explicitly to the recovery and ward nurses.
structuresAtRisk: Prostatic fossa or resection bed (catheter tip passing under the trigone)
pitfalls: The catheter tip passing into a false passage under the bladder neck after a TURP; the balloon is then inflated in the prostatic fossa.
Irrigation started without anyone recording input and output, so retained fluid goes unnoticed.
